extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, IP policymakers and practitioners assessing prior art for novelty and inventive step
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for when a disclosure (document, use, oral communication or electronic posting) constitutes prior art that can defeat novelty or inventive step in patent examination or litigation. Covers definitions, means, timing, place, evidence, internet/new media and jurisdictional nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art disclosure on patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure before the filing date or priority date may render the invention unpatentable for lack of novelty or lack of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclosure is part of the respective prior art base and it either robs the subject of novelty or makes it obvious, it will destroy patent validity. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of prior art / disclosure (Argentina Section 4(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: "All technical knowledge which has become public before the date of filing of the patent application, or, if applicable, of the recognized priority, by way of oral or written description, by use, or by any other means of disclosure or information, in the country or abroad."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argentina treats prior art broadly to include oral, written, use, or other means; no further statutory narrowing in that provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognised means of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure may occur by oral or written descriptions; use; any other means of disclosure or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New media (internet, electronic networks, email, forums) are included provided information 'became public' and was accessible without limitation. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Time requirement for prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Only disclosures made before the application date or the recognized priority date are relevant for novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relevant date is filing or priority; age of disclosure (recent or long ago) is not in itself a bar — evidence of existence and timing is required. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure generally irrelevant for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure may happen "in the country or abroad"; the place of disclosure is not relevant for patent novelty under Argentine law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions or subject-matter (e.g., utility models) may treat place differently. Australian law historically treated acts differently depending on location, though statutory changes broadened worldwide treatment. Apply domestic law to determine whether disclosure occurred. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal elements and grace periods (disclosure by inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure by the inventor or lawful successors within a statutory grace period (e.g., one year in Argentina) does not affect novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argentina: Section 5 provides 1-year grace for inventor exhibition/publication. Australia: saving provisions for recognised exhibitions, reasonable trial, disclosures without consent, etc. Whether disclosure by applicant or third party matters for applicability of these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of confidentiality agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure under an explicit or implied confidentiality agreement should be deemed not to have occurred for prior art purposes (if confidentiality maintained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If confidentiality is breached and information becomes public, it counts as disclosure; encrypted or password-protected material may avoid disclosure if access is effectively restricted. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient's ability to understand the information
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no express statutory requirements about the recipient's ability to understand the information; disclosure may be found even if recipient could not understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office or courts may consider disclosure occurred if recipient could further disseminate the information without limitation. If reverse engineering or disassembly is necessary, many groups consider that disclosure has not occurred unless there was effective public use enabling understanding. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior publication must contain an 'enabling disclosure' — enough information to enable a person skilled in the art to perform the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents must provide sufficient information and 'clear and unmistakable directions' as to each element to anticipate. If errors exist, assess whether the skilled person can fill gaps using common general knowledge. (Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on constructing a 'mosaic' for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: One may not make a 'mosaic' out of prior art information (selecting and combining isolated items across documents to create an anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires a single prior disclosure that clearly and unmistakably teaches the claimed invention; piecing together from multiple unrelated sources to create an 'anticipation' is prohibited. (Australia — 3M case referenced)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse infringement test for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A test for want of novelty asks: if the patent were valid, would the alleged anticipation constitute an infringement of it? Identify the 'essential integers' of the invention; differences limited to 'inessential integers' can mean anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify essential features; if prior art contains essential integers, it anticipates. (Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step assessment (person skilled in the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step is assessed by asking what a person skilled in the field (hypothetical, unimaginitive, uninventive) would have done faced with the problem at the priority date in light of the prior art base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the relevant field and the common general knowledge (CGK); then assess whether skilled but non-inventive person would have arrived at the claimed invention. (Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Common General Knowledge (CGK) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: CGK includes what is routinely known or used by those in the trade — the background knowledge and experience available to all those when considering making new products (3M test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CGK sets the context in which documents/acts are read for inventive step. Whether material forms part of CGK is a question of fact. (Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art for inventive step (linking rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more documents or acts can be combined only if those sources would have been reasonably expected to have been ascertained, understood and regarded as relevant to work in the relevant art by persons skilled in the art at the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related documents may be treated as a single source if the skilled person would treat them so. Mere hindsight combination is not permitted. (Australia; Argentina references similar principles)

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional treatment of pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of pending (unpublished) applications varies: some laws do not treat unpublished pending applications as prior art, while published pending applications can affect novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argentina: Section 4 does not provide that pending unpublished applications affect assessment; priority rules (Section 15) prevent double patenting. Australia: nuances exist — published pending applications can affect inventive step; some statements note pending applications, whether open to the public or not, can invalidate later applications for novelty (jurisdictional variance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and shifting of proof for internet/new media disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof that a particular piece of information was disclosed on the internet rests on the Patent Office during prosecution, or on the party who claims nullity; if applicant/plaintiff has the information easily available, burden may shift to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving precise publication dates and access on the internet can be difficult; evidence standards and who must produce evidence are important considerations. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards and manipulation concerns for new media
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential manipulation or disappearance of internet content creates evidentiary difficulties; nonetheless, manipulation does not automatically require different substantive standards for recognizing disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different levels or types of evidence may be needed to establish internet disclosures; courts/examiners decide on a case-by-case basis whether available evidence suffices. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and limitations for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: For an electronic disclosure to constitute prior art the information must have 'become public' and be accessible to the public without limitations; encryption, passwords or payment requirements may impede public availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A password/encryption/payment does not automatically prevent disclosure being prior art — assess whether public access without restrictions existed or whether recipients were bound to confidence. (Argentina; Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperless information treated equivalently to traditional disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperless/electronic information (internet, databases, email) can constitute sufficient disclosure to affect novelty or inventive step and is not treated differently in substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirements remain the same; practical peculiarities (dating, accessibility, archiving) affect proof rather than the legal standard. (Australia; Argentina)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory savings and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of disclosures may be saved from being prior art, e.g., disclosures without consent of applicant, disclosures to governments, recognised international exhibitions, disclosures to learned societies, reasonable trial by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These savings/exceptions are jurisdiction-specific and must be applied according to statute and facts. (Australia cited examples)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model/subject-matter specific rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For utility models or other subject-matters, place and timing of disclosure may be treated differently — e.g., Argentine utility model rules may allow novelty despite foreign disclosure by the applicant within six months prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check specific statutory/regulatory provisions for utility models; do not assume patent rules apply identically. (Argentina)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for applicant to establish novelty/inventive step (Australia post-amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under amendments (Patents Bill), the applicant is required to demonstrate that the subject is new and inventive on the balance of probabilities — a higher burden than earlier practice where the applicant benefited from doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a change to evidentiary burden in prosecution and affects how examiners and courts assess contested disclosures. (Australia)

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental vs intentional disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether disclosure happened accidentally or intentionally does not necessarily change its effect; however, disclosures without consent and the circumstances may engage statutory savings or affect whether the disclosure was effectively to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess facts (accessibility, distribution, consent) to determine public availability; some laws (or exceptions) may treat accidental disclosures differently in limited circumstances. (Australia; Argentina observes place not relevant but exceptions exist)

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of errors in disclosed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in disclosed information do not automatically prevent a finding of disclosure; the decisive issue is whether the disclosure effectively occurred and whether gaps can be filled by the skilled person using CGK without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case-by-case factual assessment: if errors mean insufficient teaching, novelty may survive; if skilled person can bridge gaps, disclosure may still anticipate. (Argentina; Australia)
